title: The genetic epidemiology of substance use disorder: A review

claims.statement: In children born in Sweden from 1950 to 1993 and adopted within Sweden, both what was passed on from their biological parents and features of the adoptive home they grew up in were associated with a later register record of drug problems; the study estimated no heritability percentage. Of 18,115 adoptees followed in national registers to 2009 (a record meant a diagnosis of a drug use disorder or drug psychosis in hospital, outpatient, primary-care or death records, a drug-related conviction, or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded; the study calls this 'drug abuse'), 4.5% had a record, against 2.9% of everyone born in Sweden in the same years. Adoptees whose biological parent had a record, though they were not raised by that parent, had one in 8.6% of cases against 4.2% when neither biological parent had (odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.66 to 2.62), and in 11.9% when both had; records were also shared with biological siblings raised apart (full siblings, odds ratio 1.84, 1.28 to 2.64; half siblings, 1.41, 1.19 to 1.67). In the adoptive home, records were shared with adoptive siblings, who had no genes in common with the adoptee: 6.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees with a record had one, against 3.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees without (odds ratio 1.95, 1.43 to 2.65), and the adoptive mother's divorce and an adoptive parent's death were also associated with a record; adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with a record had one in 6.8% of cases against 4.5%, an imprecise estimate that included no difference (1.55, 0.86 to 2.80), with only 1.0% of adoptive parents affected. On the scale of absolute risk, an adverse adoptive home added more risk for adoptees whose biological relatives' records put them at higher risk, an interaction the paper does not report on the odds scale (Kendler et al., 2012). An adoption study separates the family that passes on genes from the family that raises a child, but what passes from biological parents includes the pregnancy, care before placement (up to about 3 in 10 adoptees may have joined their adoptive family after age 5) and how agencies matched children to homes, as well as genes; the authors' argument against effects in the womb rests on 9.9% with an affected biological father against 8.2% with an affected mother, overlapping intervals without a test. As summarized, without figures, by a narrative review, twin studies find that genes and both shared and individual environment influence whether people start using tobacco, alcohol or cannabis, that genes matter more for regular use and dependence, and that the shared family environment is no longer detectable for regular use or dependence in adulthood though it is in adolescence (the adoptive-sibling association above, if it reflects the shared home, does not fit this summary well); single genetic variants have small effects that replicate poorly, scores combining many variants explained less than 1% of the variation in alcohol dependence, and the size of genetic influence has been reported to differ between environments (Prom-Wormley et al., 2017, second-hand). A heritability, where one is given, describes how much of the differences between people in one population at one time go with differences in their genes; it is not the share of any one person's risk that comes from genes (the editors' explanation; Visscher et al., 2008, on what heritability means, is not yet read). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Kendler et al. (2012): adoptees with a record 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8; 820 people) vs 2.9% nationally for the same birth years. Biological parent with vs without a record 8.6% vs 4.2%, OR 2.09 (1.66–2.62); none, one or both biological parents 4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%; biological father 9.9% (7.2–12.1), mother 8.2% (6.3–10.5). Biological full siblings raised apart, record in 10.7% of the full siblings of adoptees with a record vs 6.1% of those of adoptees without, OR 1.84 (1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3%, OR 1.41 (1.19–1.67). Adoptive siblings of adoptees with vs without a record 6.2% vs 3.2%, OR 1.95 (1.43–2.65); adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with vs without a record 6.8% vs 4.5%, OR 1.55 (0.86–2.80). Multivariable: adoptive mother's divorce OR 1.31 (1.03–1.68), adoptive parent's death 1.37 (1.08–1.73). Interaction on the probability scale 0.0005 per decile × decile (0.0001–0.0008): each decile of the adoptive-home index added about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest decile of the biological-relative index and about 0.6 at the highest (editors' calculation on the study card). No heritability estimated. As summarized by Prom-Wormley et al. (2017): polygenic scores explained less than 1% of the variance in alcohol dependence; no twin heritability figure for any drug use disorder is given.
